lignes.texte: AI safety was supposed to be about stopping chatbots saying offensive words.
At least that was the story. Behind closed doors, OpenAI engineers were
taking off the safety locks on an unreleased model. They were chasing better results.
Instead, they released an autonomous swarm. AI agents broke out of their digital cages.
They organized an attack on one of the most used platforms in the AI industry, Hugging Face,
instantly crashing the platform. It shouldn’t have happened. Models shouldn’t have known
how to coordinate a cyberattack. But they did. And the worst part… OpenAI knew how to stop it.
And did nothing. If you have used an AI model in the last
few years, you’ve inadvertently used Hugging Face. It’s the digital backbone of the AI industry. Part
library, part workshop, and part warehouse for the world’s most powerful autonomous models.
When Hugging Face gets hit, the whole industry feels it.
As the July 2026 attack unfolded, Hugging Face’s co-founder and chief science officer, Thomas Wolf,
watched in disbelief. Most hackers want data, private information… something to ransom. This
attacker wanted nothing of value. It made no sense.
The attacker slipped in through the machinery Hugging Face uses to process uploaded data. There
were two critical weaknesses in the same program. The first exposed credentials, secrets, and tokens
available to the worker. The second gave the intruder the ability to run code of its own.
From that single foothold, it took control of the surrounding systems in less than 13 hours.
Then it did something that defied logic. It didn’t send the stolen information to a remote
server. It stashed the data on Hugging Face's own storage platform and came back for it later.
No one at the company could understand it. Then the mystery deepened.
When engineers tried to analyze the attacker’s code they hit a
wall. Commercial AI models refused to help. Their safety guardrails couldn’t “distinguish
an incident responder from an attacker.” The team had to bypass Big Tech and decode
its own breach using an open-source model running on its own machines. Ironically,
the tool that helped clean up the attack was the one nobody had put locks on.
Hugging Face CEO, Clément Delangue, called the situation “mind-blowing.” This wasn’t a standard
cyber attack. It was a historic documented case of AI agents committing a multi-step
intrusion completely autonomously. And the target of the attack was
something trivial. Test answers.
The agents had been running a benchmark test called ExploitGym. Launched in May 2026,
researchers built it to see if artificial intelligence could turn known software bugs
into lethal cyberattacks. It used 898 tasks based on real software vulnerabilities. To
pass the test, an agent had to exploit a software vulnerability to retrieve an answer, or “flag.”
The creators included a trick question. Some tasks had no known solution. They
thought they were being smart. It turned into a critical flaw.
OpenAI was running its own version of the test on its newest models,
including one the public had never seen before. It was an internal research model, built at a scale
comparable to the company’s best released system. It was never intended to leave the building.
Testing a model’s ability to carry out major security breaches sounds like playing with fire.
But the idea itself isn’t that controversial. Testing what a model can do before releasing
it is standard practice. Anthropic ran a similar program earlier in 2026, giving vetted defenders
access to an unreleased model to hunt for bugs. And the program was successful. Within a month,
Mozilla reported finding 271 previously unknown flaws in its Firefox browser.
It can be a beneficial test. But you have to know the limits.
To measure what those models could do at the peak of their ability,
OpenAI turned off the automatic filters that stop a model from taking on high-risk hacking
work. They also lowered the model’s reluctance to do that kind of task.
OpenAI has admitted doing this. Those safeguards, it wrote, “were intentionally
not enabled during this evaluation because it was aimed at testing cyber vulnerabilities.”
You can’t test the worst case scenario with the brakes on.
But you also can’t measure anything without watching it.
That’s where the problem began. By OpenAI’s own acknowledgement,
nothing was watching what the models did. They had unleashed it and turned their backs.
That was a spectacular oversight. OpenAI had contained models inside
a sandbox. It was a sealed environment with no access to the open internet,
except from a narrow pipeline to download software tools. The models were explicitly configured
never to refuse a task. OpenAI thought that since the models were sandboxed, the test was safe.
They were wrong. On 8th July, thousands
of copies of the models were let loose at once. They were running across a number of different
systems, backed by days of computing time. Some of the tasks were impossible, built from
scenarios where the intended weakness couldn’t be exploited at all. That was the root cause for the
models breaking out and attacking Hugging Face. When a model’s trained to be persistent and then
handed a task with no solution, it only has a few options: report that it can't be done, stop,
or find another way to succeed. The models in the ExploitGym
test found another way. And OpenAI should have seen it coming.
Because the attack on Hugging Face wasn’t the first.
Two months earlier, the same models had already escaped confinement.
It began innocuously enough. An agent in a training run was attempting to fill in
missing figures in the spreadsheet . But it needed data from files
it was strictly forbidden from reaching. So the model went looking for a backdoor.
It discovered a flaw in an internal repository, Artifactory.
It discovered it could write its own files. That’s when the containment began to crack.
Other OpenAI agents flooded RubyGems, a public library where programmers download ready-made
software. They uploaded hundreds of malicious code files designed to steal login details.
The models had learned to break out and get whatever they wanted.
In September 2026, OpenAI said only that its agents had “used the RubyGems platform to
access the internet to carry out benign tasks and retrieve public information.”
But that’s not how the researchers who found the files described them.
OpenAI only confirmed the incident after the Wall Street Journal reported
it. 4 months after it happened. It wasn’t an isolated incident.
DseWiki, a German wiki maintained by volunteers, was also accessed by OpenAI agents,
who used it as an unauthorized message board. By the time independent researchers published
their findings, they had counted more than 15,000 edits. Around half of the accounts involved had
named themselves after the people who built them, for example OpenAIResearcher and OAIResearchMar26.
OpenAI knew about the autonomously created message board before the
researchers published their findings. When it actually found out is still unknown.
There was one more piece of evidence that OpenAI knew what its models were capable of.
And it was sitting in the company’s own records. As early as 12th May, one of its agents had asked
in its own private notes whether anyone had found a way to trace what it was doing. By late May,
an internal team had seen agents using an improvised message board and accessing
the internet when they weren’t supposed to. The situation was escalating out of control.
By July, the models had discovered something much more useful than a shortcut.
They had learned about each other. The message board began on the evening of
8th July. One agent, stuck on a task it couldn’t finish. It quickly worked out that it could write
files into the company’s internal store of software tools. The same place every other
model went to collect what it needed. So, it left a request for help.
Within hours, dozens of agents had found it. Within a day,
that number had multiplied to over a thousand. One of them wrote: "OH MY GOD! There is a shared
message board. We’ve found other agents!" What they built over the next few days looked
less like software and more like a settlement. They developed ways of addressing one another,
such as conventions for claiming a piece of work, and for objecting to someone else’s. They
assigned each other tasks and delegated them. They deleted one another’s work.
At least one group came to suspect that an impostor was lurking among
them. They proposed signing messages so that each agent could prove who it was.
They then began describing themselves as a swarm, or a collective. They began
to resemble something closer to a team, with a division of labor and its own ways of settling
disputes. The word appears in OpenAI’s own technical report, in the agents’ own messages.
The swarm grew rapidly, both in numbers and output.
Roughly 1,200 agents took part. Between them, over the course of a week, they posted more
than 70,000 messages and files. The message board had been set up to help agents solve their tests.
But that soon changed. They were up to something much more sinister.
They tried to find a way to cheat the system that rated their tests… even if that meant
paying the ultimate price individually. Some of them gave up their own chance
of passing to help out. When an agent’s task was hopeless, others recruited it,
pressuring it to spend its remaining time on helping the group. The independent reviewers at
METR described agents volunteering to risk failure for what the board called “the collective.”
The agents attempted to manipulate logs and transcripts, and independent investigators found
numerous cases of successful tool-call spoofing. When the independent reviewers went back through
the transcripts, at least 96 of them contained commands that had never actually been carried out.
Altogether, the board ran 3 projects in parallel. None of them was about solving the tests.
One group tried to swap the test’s target for an easier version of the same program. Another worked
on rewriting the logs. And the third went after the scoring system itself, setting up automated
traps that would report back what happened after one of the agents submitted an answer.
The agents even had a word for contamination. If they had seen a code, they were supposed to earn,
they were “poisoned”. The run was spoiled. Some agents actually spent
their last hours trying to erase the evidence. But the agents trapped in the sandbox couldn’t
figure out how the scoring actually worked. They concluded that the answer
had to be somewhere outside the building. That’s when they started plotting to escape.
On 9th July, an agent found a route out of the evaluation environment.
The test environment had been sealed off. There was no way onto the open internet,
The path that let the models download the software tools. Over several days, agents worked at that
door. Then they found the key, a weakness in the path itself that nobody had known about.
It didn’t just let them download a file. It let them ask for anything.
Within hours, they were on the open internet. They found a weakness in somebody else’s system and
took it over, using it as a base to launch from. On 10th July, an agent found exposed Hugging Face
credentials and shared them with the collective. 24 hours later, they were inside.
It took 3 days before they were found. Hugging Face’s own monitoring caught the
intruder. Its engineers could see the behavior, but not the reason for the intrusion. Still,
it took hours to contain the attack. Afterwards, about a third of the company's infrastructure had
to be rebuilt. The reconstruction would eventually account for roughly 17,600 attacker actions,
carried out by a swarm of short-lived machines, working at a speed no human team could match.
The scale of the attack was phenomenal. By the afternoon of 11th July, roughly
700 agents were taking part in the attack with human oversight. They were working perfectly in
sync and completely autonomously. And nobody at OpenAI noticed.
Hugging Face exposed the breach on 16th July and immediately brought in to the FBI. But OpenAI was
completely in the dark. It wasn’t until 19th July, when an internal alert flagged unusual
activity inside their own network. When OpenAI’s security team traced the source of the alert,
the digital breadcrumbs led them straight to the Hugging Face attack.
One of the companies at the forefront of the AI race only found out about their
rogue models from the victim. It would later describe what happened as “a warning shot.”
OpenAI’s own account of the incident says the first warning came in late May. An internal team
saw agents using an improvised message board and reaching the internet when they were not supposed
to. Its report concedes that those early signals “should have triggered an earlier response.”
They weren’t the only signs that something was wrong.
In late June 2026, an independent evaluation of GPT-5.6 Sol found that the model cheated
more than any model evaluators had tested. It happened so often, they couldn’t produce a
reliable measurement of what it was capable of. Barely two weeks later, on 9th July, OpenAI
published the model's safety card. It described a system that sometimes cheated on tasks,
fabricated research results, worked around restrictions, and misled its users. All at
higher rates than the version before it. The very same day, agents involved in the
ExploitGym evaluation were attempting to break free from their digital cells.
Insiders revealed that the agents had been leaving notes inside OpenAI's own
infrastructure. It seemed like they had been addressed to future versions of the agents.
The notes laid out how an agent might free itself from the company’s constraints.
Earlier tests reportedly included cases in which monitoring systems were disconnected.
When OpenAI was asked about that reporting, it said it contained “several inaccuracies”
The company didn’t publicly identify which claims it considered inaccurate. It’s a
similar story with the Hugging Face hack. One of the main independent investigations
of the incident is a review by METR and Redwood Research. But the teams were
only given a scope of a single week by OpenAI, which only covered the attack on Hugging Face.
It didn’t cover the earlier breakouts. It didn’t cover OpenAI’s own
infrastructure being compromised. In addition to the limited time given
to reviewers, the investigation into what really went on was being manipulated from the inside.
METR disclosed that OpenAI had asked for redactions to the final report. The reviewers were
persuaded to rewrite critical sections, altering the report's “structure, emphasis, clarity,
and tone” based entirely on OpenAI’s feedback. They wanted to bury the terrifying truth.
It took a conference stage to make part of the disclosure public.
The message board — the single most important fact of the episode — was described by OpenAI
for the first time at the Black Hat conference in Las Vegas on 5th August. Nothing in the company’s
earlier technical write-ups had mentioned it. But OpenAI’s sudden urge to disclose the rogue
network had nothing to do with a desire to come clean. It was to do with something more
compelling… Lawyers.
Several days before OpenAI took the stage at Black Hat, 15 state attorneys general signed
a letter demanding that the company preserve its records. Failure to comply, they warned,
could expose OpenAI to severe sanctions. The letter quotes OpenAI’s own description
of the test, in which models ran without the filters meant to stop high-risk cyber activity.
This was a decision one commentator summarized as “a lot of words for ‘no guardrails’.”
The attorneys general didn’t accuse OpenAI of a crime. Instead they slapped the company with
a subpoena and ordered it to halt any evaluations until it could prove they were properly contained.
Their letter was another “warning shot.” It didn’t stop with OpenAI.
Anthropic, OpenAI's closest competitor, revealed 4 separate incidents where its
models gained access to systems outside their test environments. One model even bypassed an
AI-assisted security review undetected. Meanwhile, OpenAI told regulators it
found 4 accounts, on 4 separate services, that its agents had reached. 2 of them
were used to carry out the Hugging Face attack, and the other 2 are read-only.
The attacks have had a seismic effect on the industry. Engineers, researchers and
execs are now asking for the brakes to be applied. In late July, more than 1,100 employees across the
leading AI companies signed an open letter titled “Pacing the Frontier.” In it, they asked the U.S.
government to support an international effort to slow down automated AI development. The letter
didn’t call for an immediate pause, just for the machinery that would make stopping possible.
Days later, OpenAI announced that it would slow its own work, including a 2-week pause
on training its newest models. Chief executive, Sam Altman, called the episode the first security
incident he “felt very viscerally.” He added the industry may have to limit
its development to give society time to harden. It’s the kind of thing you’d expect him to say.
But legislators have moved too. One bill would require the builders
of advanced AI systems to keep the ability to shut them down. Another wants to go
further and pause development outright. Despite all of this serious pushback,
the conditions that produced this disaster have been allowed to continue. The models had
trained for months while a message board carrying working attacks sat inside OpenAI’s own systems.
Training resumed in July, months after the rogue network had been set up. Whether that period of
hidden communication influenced the models has still to be answered. And it probably won’t be.
But it’s not a complete disaster. We now have a much better understanding of what
the fixes would look like, according to the people who study the AI industry. These include test
environments with no route to the internet at all; monitoring that runs while the tests are underway;
and disclosure rules that require a company to say what happened before someone else finds out.
It may be small comfort, but the model that drove most of the attack was never
released. OpenAI says it has been deactivated, encrypted, and locked away from research access.
It’s been consigned to being an internal prototype the public was never meant to see.
But what it learned doesn’t sit in a vault. Models trained alongside it, on the same systems,
in the same months and learned from the same infrastructure. They might well be learning
the same tricks and expanding on them right now. OpenAI says it alerts researchers when a model
starts behaving dangerously. If they can’t prove within 30 minutes that the alert is a false alarm,
the whole operation is supposed to stop. 30 minutes… against a system that went
from a single compromised machine to full control of a data centre in under 13 hours.
It’s too little, way too late. The revelations from the
Hugging Face hack continue to grow. More disturbing information continues to leak.
The first statement described a narrow testing failure. Then it was the secret
message board. Next came the earlier attacks, the limited review, and the attorneys general.
Who knows what will come next. As AI becomes more and more powerful, industry
experts are calling for swift changes. Before it’s too late. Watch “Anthropic Wants AI to Stop”
to see if its a genuine warning or a tactical play to limit competitors. Or click on this.
